Written Exam

Exam consisting of 8 learning test sections assessing knowledge and understanding of the
Organization Theory and Design topics.
Each section, not more than 25 minutes, will be independently graded
Threshold to pass is 18/30 an maximum Mark is 30/30.
The final mark is obtained as the average of marks given to each section of the written
exam: 0,25 rounded to the superior number
Each Test consists of 30 multiple choice questions with 4 possible alternatives.
Each correct answer adds 1 point, for each wrong answer you take off a point, if you do
not answer the score remains unchanged.
In some Tests some questions are replaced by twice as many statements that require you
to indicate as a true/false answer. For true/false answers you add or subtract 0.5.
Example of questions will be available for each Learning Test.

Sections of Learning Test are:
LEARNING TEST 1: Chapter 1 and 2
LEARNING TEST 2: Chapter 3
LEARNING TEST 3: Chapter 4, 5 and 6
LEARNING TEST 4: Chapter 7
LEARNING TEST 5: Chapter 8
LEARNING TEST 6: Chapter 9 and 10
LEARNING TEST 7: Chapter 11
LEARNING TEST 8: Chapter 12 and 13
There is the possibility to take the learning tests, 2 at a time, after the related topics have
been completed, during the course of Organization Theory and Design during the lessons.

Exam Information

 Prof. Piercarlo Dondi – A.Y. 2025/26

Exam Structure

 The exam is written, and it is composed by two sections:
 Theory (up to 20 points)
 Programming in Python (up to 10 points)

 The grade will be the sum of the two sections
 NOTE: 30L is achieved with a very well explained theory and well-
 structured code

 IMPORTANT: to pass the exam is necessary to reach a
 sufficient score in both Theory (>= 12 points) and
 Programming (>=6 points)

 IMPORTANT: non-running or empty code means exam
 failed

 Approximate duration: 2h and 20m

 Piercarlo Dondi – Algorithms and Data Structures: Exam Information – A.Y. 2025/26 2

Exam Structure – Details

 Theory:
 Open questions and/or multiple choices on all the topics discussed
 during the course, both long (e.g., explain Dijkstra’s algorithm) and
 short (e.g., when it is possible to apply Dijkstra’s algorithm?)
 Practical exercises as seen during lectures (e.g., perform Dijkstra’s
 algorithm on a given graph)

 Programming in Python:
 Solve a short problem applying the concepts seen during the course
 It is enough to find a reasonable solution for the problem, not the
 most efficient one
 Basic data structures (e.g., stack or queue) will be provided
 IMPORTANT: an improper use of a data structure will lower the
 score, while a well-structured code will raise it
 IMPORTANT: it is not allowed to modify the problem conditions
 (e.g., transform a tree into a list to simplify the assigned task)
 IMPORTANT: the default editor used for the exam is IDLE

 Boolean expressions

 A boolean expression has two possible values:
 I true
 I false

 In Python, a boolean expression/variable belong to type bool and
 the values are:
 I True

 Examples:

 Relational operators

 x == y # x is equal to y
 x != y # x is not equal to y
 x > y # x is greater than y
 x < y # x is less than y
 x >= y # x is greater than or equal to y
 x <= y # x is less than or equal to y

 Very common mistake:
 I = instead of ==

 Logical operators

 x and y # True if both are True
 x or y # True unless both are False
 not x # True if x is False and viceversa

 I Short-circuit evaluation:
 I the evaluation of a logical expression is stopped as soon as the
 result is clear
 I not every operand is evaluated
 I 3 > 5 and x > 0 is False
 I 3 < 5 and x > 0 is x > 0
 I Execution is faster, but side effects in the operands evaluation
 can not take place (e.g., when functions are involved)
 I The operands order is important:
 I x/y > 3 and y != 0: the operands must be switched
 I Operands should be bool, but Python considers True any
 non-zero value

 I Conditional statements allow to change the behaviour of the
 program depending on the context

 I condition

 Structured programming

 I In structured programming, the programs are composition of
 control structures
 I sequence, selection, repetition
 I This is enough for implementing any computable function
 I i.e., any algorithm
 I Turing-computable functions
 I Church–Turing thesis: computable functions are those that can
 be effectively computed by a “mechanical” device using limited
 resources and time

 I In class Triangle:
 I def draw(self, ttl):
 """ Draw the triangle using the turtle ttl """
 # compute the absolute position of the vertices
 vertices_abs = []
 for v in self.vertices:
 vertices_abs.append(self.origin + v)
 ttl.penup()
 # position the turtle on the last vertex
 ttl.goto(vertices_abs[-1].x, vertices_abs[-1].y)
 ttl.pendown()
 for v in vertices_abs:
 tl.goto(v.x, v.y)

 I Notes on Triangle.draw():
 I Instead of using the angle-and-distance notation to drive the
 turtle, the goto() method can be used to exploit the vertices
 notation.
 I Alternatively, the math module can be imported and the need
 quantities can be easily calculated.
 I To this aim, the absolute coordinates of the vertices are
 computed.
 I Then the turtle is positioned on the last vertex, resulting in the
 draving of the side between the last and the first vertices when
 the first goto() is called in the loop.
 I Alternatively, the turtle can be positioned on the first vertex
 and the loop run in the reverse order
 (for v in vertices_abs[::-1]).
 I Or the first vertex can be appended to the the vertices list and
 the loop run as it is.

 I Game of Life (John Horton Conway, 1970) is game to simulate

 I every cell interacts only with its eight neighbors:

 I any live cell having two or three neighbors survive
 I any live cell having more than three neighbors dies
 (overpopulation)
 I any dead cell having exactly three neighbors becomes a live
 cell (reproduction)

(2)

 x and y # True if both are True
 x or y # True unless both are False
 not x # True if x is False and viceversa

 ▶ Short-circuit evaluation:
 ▶ the evaluation of a logical expression is stopped as soon as the
 result is clear
 ▶ not every operand is evaluated
 ▶ 3 > 5 and x > 0 is False
 ▶ 3 < 5 and x > 0 is x > 0
 ▶ Execution is faster, but side effects in the operands evaluation
 can not take place (e.g., when functions are involved)
 ▶ The operands order is important:
 ▶ x/y > 3 and y != 0: the operands must be switched
 ▶ Operands should be bool, but Python considers True any
 non-zero value

 Rules for using recursion:

 + It allows for a simple implementation
 − It may require more computational resources than the
 corresponding iterative solution

 tuple assignment
 ▶ Swapping the value of two variables is a common operation:
 >>> temp = a
 >>> a = b
 >>> b = temp
 ▶ Tuple assignment is more elegant:
 >>> a, b = b, a
 ▶ left side: tuple of variables
 ▶ right side: tuple of expressions
 ▶ first evaluate all the expressions, then make the assignments
 ▶ Cardinality of left and right sides must be the same:
 >>> a, b = 1, 2, 3
 ValueError: too many values to unpack
 ▶ Right side can be any kind of sequence (e.g., a list):
 >>> addr = 'monty@python.org'
 >>> uname, domain = addr.split('@')

 Tuples from dictionaries
 ▶ The method called items() returns a sequence of tuples,
 where each tuple is a key-value pair:
 >>> d = {'a': 0, 'b': 1, 'c': 2}
 >>> t = d.items()
 >>> t
 dict_items([('c', 2), ('a', 0), ('b', 1)])
 ▶ The result is a dict_items object, which is an iterator that
 iterates the key-value pairs:
 >>> for key, value in d.items():
 print(key, value)
 c 2
 a 0
 b 1
 ▶ the order of the key can be any
 ▶ but since Python 3.7 is the insertion order

 Dictionaries from tuples

 ▶ Using a list of tuples to initialize a new dictionary:
 >>> t = [('a', 0), ('c', 2), ('b', 1)]
 >>> d = dict(t)
 >>> d
 {'a': 0, 'c': 2, 'b': 1}
 ▶ Combining dict with zip yields a concise way to create a
 dictionary from sequences:
 >>> d = dict(zip('abc', range(3)))
 >>> d
 {'a': 0, 'c': 2, 'b': 1}
 ▶ The dictionary method update() also takes a list of tuples
 and adds them, as key-value pairs, to an existing dictionary.

 ▶ def draw(self, ttl):
 """ Draw the triangle using the turtle ttl """
 # compute the absolute position of the vertices
 vertices_abs = []
 for v in self.vertices:
 vertices_abs.append(self.origin + v)
 ttl.penup()
 # position the turtle on the last vertex
 ttl.goto(vertices_abs[-1].x, vertices_abs[-1].y)
 ttl.pendown()
 for v in vertices_abs:
 tl.goto(v.x, v.y)

 ▶ Notes on Triangle.draw():
 ▶ Instead of using the angle-and-distance notation to drive the
 turtle, the goto() method can be used to exploit the vertices
 notation.
 ▶ Alternatively, the math module can be imported and the need
 quantities can be easily calculated.
 ▶ To this aim, the absolute coordinates of the vertices are
 computed.
 ▶ Then the turtle is positioned on the last vertex, resulting in the
 draving of the side between the last and the first vertices when
 the first goto() is called in the loop.
 ▶ Alternatively, the turtle can be positioned on the first vertex
 and the loop run in the reverse order
 (for v in vertices_abs[::-1]).
 ▶ Or the first vertex can be appended to the the vertices list and
 the loop run as it is.

 Collision

 ▶ The ball collides against boundary side if the circle center is
 closer to a rectangle side for less than the radius.
 ▶ The constraint in the boundary is realized by testing the value
 of the center of the ball and set it properly if its components
 exceeds the boundary values:

 if ball.y < -maxY+ball.radius:
 ball.y = -maxY+ball.radius
 if ball.y > maxY-ball.radius:
 ball.y = maxY-ball.radius

 """ Draw the triangle using the turtle ttl """
 # compute the absolute position of the vertices
 vertices_abs = []

 ttl.penup()
 # position the turtle on the last vertex
 ttl.goto(vertices_abs[-1].x, vertices_abs[-1].y)
 ttl.pendown()
 for v in vertices_abs:
 tl.goto(v.x, v.y)

 evaluated several times.

 always the same.

 return L

 >>> q = a_list()

 Storing the game resources

 ▶ When the number of images for the games, or other resources
 as well, is high, collecting them in a dedicated directory or a
 tree of directories is suggested.
 ▶ Having hundreds of images with very similar name or naming
 the files including metainformation like name of the character,
 status, and index in the sequence can be uncomfortable.
 ▶ The path can be structured as:
 ▶ name of the type of resources (e.g., 'sprites')
 ▶ name of the type of element (e.g., 'bsprite')
 ▶ name of the status and position in the sequence (e.g.,
 'right-1.gif')
 ▶ The image path can then be reconstructed programmatical,
 using os.path.join() function.
 ▶ os.path.join('sprites', 'bsprite', 'right-1.gif')
 ▶ It is better to use join for portability reasons: it adds the
 proper separator given the current OS.

 Global variables

 ▶ In the previous program, known is a variable defined outside
 the function fibonacci_memo(), but accessible inside.
 ▶ Technically, known belongs to the frame called __main__
 ▶ a memory space defined automatically for the main module
 ▶ Such a variable is called global (variable)
 ▶ a function that belong to the __main__ scope
 ▶ Every function can see a global variable and can use its value.
 ▶ known can be modified from inside the function because it is a
 dict object that is mutable.
 ▶ Only mutable global variables can be modified from the inside
 of a function.

 Local memo

 ▶ Passage of the memo variable as parameter avoids the need of
 global variable:
 def fibonacci_fast(n, known={0: 0, 1: 1}):
 if n in known:
 return known[n]
 else:
 res = fibonacci_fast(n-1, known) + \
 fibonacci_fast(n-2, known)
 known[n] = res # memo update
 return res

 fibonacci_fast() can be invoked simply:

 Sorting on multiple keys

 ▶ For example, given a list of three-valued tuples:
 L = [(1, 5, 9), (2, 4, 7), (1, 6, 7), (1, 5, 8)]

 1. on the first element, ascending
 2. on the second element, descending
 3. on the third element, descending

 Serialization
 ▶ Data structures such as strings, lists, or tuples are ordered
 because they have a sequential structure:
 ▶ (1, 2,

3) is False
 ▶ Dictionaries, instead, are unordered:
 ▶ {'a': 1, 'b': 2} == {'b': 2, 'a': 1} is True

 ▶ To be stored or transmitted (e.g., in a text file), a data
 structure must be translated in a sequential format.
 ▶ And eventually in a sequence of bytes.
 ▶ This operation is called serialization (or marshalling).
 ▶ The opposite operation is called deserialization (or
 unmarshalling).
 ▶ Formats like JSON and YAML are commonly used for data
 serialization.
 ▶ JSON is implemented in the Python Standard Library.
 ▶ YAML module inclusion is under discussion.

 with statement
 ▶ The usage of an external source requires some operations to
 handle its management.
 ▶ e.g., files: open(), close().
 ▶ The with statement allows to create a context in which the
 focus is on the operation logic, not on resource management.
 ▶ Syntax:
 with <expression> [as <target>]:
 <body>

 ▶ def draw(self):
 """ Draw the triangle using the turtle """
 # compute the absolute position of the vertices
 vertices_abs = []

 # position the turtle on the last vertex
 goto(vertices_abs[-1].x, vertices_abs[-1].y)
 pendown()
 for v in vertices_abs:

 ▶ Notes on Triangle.draw():
 ▶ Instead of using the angle-and-distance notation to drive the
 turtle, the goto() method can be used to exploit the vertices
 notation.
 ▶ Alternatively, the math module can be imported and the need
 quantities can be easily calculated.
 ▶ To this aim, the absolute coordinates of the vertices are
 computed.
 ▶ Then the turtle is positioned on the last vertex, resulting in the
 drawing of the side between the last and the first vertices when
 the first goto() is called in the loop.
 ▶ Alternatively, the turtle can be positioned on the first vertex
 and the loop run in the reverse order
 (for v in vertices_abs[::-1]).
 ▶ Or the first vertex can be appended to the the vertices list and
 the loop run as it is.

BOTTOM-UP Proof Procedure

Reminder: A fact is just a rule without a body!

KB:

1. free_drink(Y) :- bar_owner(X), friend(X, Y).
2. friend(X, Z) :- friend(X, Y), friend(Y, Z).
3. friend(X, Y) :- friend(Y, X).
4. bar_owner(alice).
5. friend(alice, bob).
6. friend(bob, carol).

Step 1: Initialization

C = { }

Step 2:

Select clause 4.
 bar_owner(alice) :- (empty body) .

 Condition: Is there a substitution sigma such that, applied to the body
 of our clause, gives us atoms that are already in C?

 In this case the body is empty!!

 The condition is satisfied TRIVIALLY, because the body is empty!

 The head of the rule: bar_owner(alice)
 is not already in C!

 So We can add bar_owner(alice) to C

C = { bar_owner(alice) }

Step 3:

Select 5. friend(alice, bob).

Again, the clause has no body. We can add the head to C, since it is not already there

C = { bar_owner(alice), friend(alice, bob) }

Step 4:

Select 6. friend(bob, carol).

Same as before, it is a fact.
C = { bar_owner(alice), friend(alice, bob), friend(bob, carol).}

Step 5:
continuing with the other rules:

1. free_drink(Y) :- bar_owner(X), friend(X, Y).
2. friend(X, Z) :- friend(X, Y), friend(Y, Z). (transitivity!)
3. friend(X, Y) :- friend(Y, X).

Select clause 3. friend(X, Y) :- friend(Y, X).
Define s = {Y/alice, X/bob}
Body under the application of s: s(friend(Y, X)) = friend(alice, bob)
This is inside C!
So we can add s(head) = s(friend(X, Y)) = friend(bob, alice) to C

-> C = { bar_owner(alice), friend(alice, bob), friend(bob, carol) }

```
parent_of(alice, carol). parent_of(bob, carol).

person(X) :- parent_of(X, Y). % domain of parent_of
person(Y) :- parent_of(X, Y). % range of parent_of

% child_of is the inverse of parent_of
child_of(X, Y) :- parent_of(Y, X).
```

## Modeling reflexivity

Modeling reflexivity for `loves`. Intuitively this should work:
```
loves(X, X).
```
This fact (i.e., rule without a body) is however *usafe*.
DLV requires that variables that appear in the head of a rule (like `X` in
`loves(X, X)`) also appear in a positive predicate in the body of the rule
(i.e., a predicate not under the scope of negation as failure).

We can fix the rule as follows:
`loves(X, X) :- person(X). % SAFE`

## Modeling asymmetry and irreflexivity

Add a constraint that enforces that `parent_of` is asymmetric.
Meaning: whenever `parent_of(X, Y)`, then it is impossible that `parent_of(Y, X)`.
Or: `parent_of(X, Y)` and `parent_of(Y, X)` cannot be true at the same time:
```
:- parent_of(X, Y), parent_of(Y, X).
```

`parent_of` is irreflexive:
```
:- parent_of(X, X).
```

## Modeling functionality

The predicate `spouse` is functional if every `X` has at most one spouse, i.e.,
whenever `spouse(X, Y)` and `spouse(X, Z)` are true, then `Y` and `Z` must be
equal: `Y = Z`.

This would suggest the following solution:
`Y = Z :- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z).`
This is however incorrect, since Datalog/DLV does not support equality in the
head of a rule.

Equivalently, we can express that it is impossible for an `X` to have spouses
`Y` and `Z` different from each other at the same time, with a constraint:
```
:- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z), Y != Z.
```

This means that if in our KB we have:
```
spouse(alice, bob).
spouse(alice, david).
```
Then DLV is going to give an empty output: the KB is inconsistent.

However, what if we have `spouse(alice, bob).` and `spouse(alice, robert).`?
We could imagine that `bob` and `robert` are different *names* for the same
person, and so our KB should not be inconsistent.

Datalog however assumes the *unique name assumption*: constants with a different
name refer to different things/entities. So, according to Datalog, `bob` and
`robert` must be different people.

We can try to circumvent this assumption by removing the constraint above
(i.e., `:- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z), Y != Z.`), and instead modeling our own
equality relation, defining the predicate `same_as` as an equivalence relation
(reflexive, symmetric, and transitive):
```
same_as(X, X) :- person(X). % Reflexivity
same_as(X, Y) :- same_as(Y, X). % Symmetry
same_as(X, Y) :- same_as(X, Z), same_as(Z, Y). % Transitivity
```

Now we can model functionality as follows:
`same_as(Y, Z) :- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z).`

So, if we have
```
spouse(alice, bob).
spouse(alice, robert).
```
then DLV will infer `same_as(bob, robert)`.
1. Compute the grounding of P if P is not ground (i.e., if P contains variables).
2. Come up with candidate answer sets S (this is often the difficult part!)
3. Compute the GL transormation of Ground(P) wrt S, resulting in the program P'
4. Verify whether S is an answer set of P'
5. If S is an answer set of P', then it is also an answer set of P!

6. Test other candidate solutions! There might be multiple answer sets.
       I.e., go back to step 2.

How to perform step 2? A few hints:

    - Every answer set must contain the facts of the program.
    - Every answer set must also contain whatever can be directly inferred from
      the facts through positive rules (no negation as failure)
    - If there is a disjunction, this means that there *may* be multiple answer
      sets, one for each disjunct. E.g., a disjunction p v q may lead to an
      answer set containing p, and an answer set containing q.
    - Try to perform some kind of informal bottom-up reasoning.
        (also possibly involving NAF rules, but be careful)
    - If nothing works:
        Start from any candidate answer set (but at least include the facts).
        Perform steps 3 and 4. If anything goes wrong, try to understand why
        (e.g., maybe your candidate answer set is missing a few atoms that are
        needed to satisfy a rule). If something goes wrong, it gives you hints
        on how you can revise your initial candidate solution.

    ***********************************************************************
    * Try to do all of the exercises on your own, or come up with new     *
    * programs to test.                                                   *
    * The best way is to try on many examples,                            *
    * so that you develop an intuition on how this works.                 *
    * You can test your programs with DLV, but first try without DLV!     *
    ***********************************************************************

    2. bird(X) :- penguin(X).

First step: compute the grounding

Two constants: tweety, pingu.

Ground(P):

    1. fly(tweety) :- bird(tweety), not penguin(tweety).
    2. fly(pingu) :- bird(pingu), not penguin(pingu).
    3. bird(tweety) :- penguin(tweety).
    4. bird(pingu) :- penguin(pingu).
    5. bird(tweety).
    6. penguin(pingu).

Second step: intuitively come up with a candidate answer set.

Candidate answer set S = {
                           bird(tweety),   % added because it is a fact
                           penguin(pingu), % added because it is a fact
                           bird(pingu),    % inferable from fact and rule 4
                           fly(tweety)     % Why? See (*) below

Exercise 1.2

Program P: `p :- not p.`

Candidates:

- `S1 = {}`: NOT an AS.
 Taking the GL(P, S1), we delete `not p` from the body, and all that is left is `p.`
 S1 is not a model of GL(P, S1), because it does not satisfy the fact `p` => not an answer set.

- `S2 = {p}`: NOT an AS
 Taking the GL of P = `p :- not p.`,
 because the body of the only rule contains `not p`,
 and `p` is in our candidate solution S2,
 then we must remove the whole rule `p :- not p.`, so that
 `GL(P, S2)` is an empty program: a program with no facts and rules.

 Is S2 an answer set of `GL(P, S2)`?
 1. Is S2 a model of the GL(P, S2)? True, because there is nothing to
 satisfy, so all the rules of GL(P, S2) are trivially/vacuously satisfied.
 2. Consistency: S2 is consistent.
 3. S2 is not however NOT an AS because of minimality: a proper subset of S2,
 namely the empty set {}, is alrready an answer set of GL(P, S2).

 VERY IMPORTANT NOTE:
 The fact that the empty set {} is an answer set of GL(P, S2)
 does NOT mean that {} is an answer set of the whole initial program P.

 REMEMBER THE GENERAL RULE:
 If X is an answer set of GL(P, X), then it is an answer set of the whole program P.
 <-- Note that the candidate answer set and the set used to compute the GL
 of P MUST BE THE SAME in order for this rule to work (X in this case).

 So, in order for {} to be an answer set of the program p, it should be an answer set of GL(P, {})!
 But we have already seen that S1={} is not an answer set of GL(P, S1) =
 GL(P, {}). So {} cannot be an answer set!

 ---> The fact that {} is an answer set of GL(P, S2), i.e. of the program <---
 ---> obtained by taking the GL of P with respect to a *different* candidate S2, <---
 ---> does not tell us anything. <---

Another candidate:
- `S3 = {-p}`: Not an answer set.
 GL(P, S3): Delete `not p` (because `p` is not in S3), and so we are left
 with simply `p`. S3 is not a model of the GL(P, S3).

Note: Sometimes there are no answer sets for a program!

Exercise 3

Program P:
`a :- not b.`

Candidates (going brute-force again):

- S1 = {}: NOT an answer set.
 GL(P, S1): Considering the only rule `a :- not b`,
 because `b` is not in S1,
 then `b` "fails" to be true,
 so `not b` is true, meaning that we can remove it from the rule.
 All we are left with is the program `GL(P, S1)` = {`a.`}
 S1 is not a model of the resulting program.

- S2 = {a}: YES, an answer set.
 GL(P, S2): {a}
 S2 is a model, it is consistent, and it is minimal.

- S3 = {b}
 GL(P, S3).
 Considering the only rule `a :- not b`,
 Since `b` is inside S3,
 then `not b` is false.
 The whole rule `a :- not b` is true/satisfied, since its body is
 satisfied. So we can forget about it, and delete it.
 The resulting program GL(P, S3) is the empty program, and
 S3 = {b} is not a *minimal* model, since the empty set is a model of
 the empty program.

- S4 = {a, b}
 GL(P, S4) = {}
 S4 = {a, b} is not a *minimal* model, again.

To sum up: the only answer set is S2 = {a}.

Exercise 9

```
p :- not p, d .
q v r :- not d.
d :- not r.
-q.
```

Let's build our candidate answer set step by step.
For sure, we start by adding the fact: `S = {-q}`. We can now try reasoning
rule-by-rule, since going brute-force would take too long.

- Consider `p :- not p, d .`
 - What if we add `p` to our candidate `S`? Then this rule will be deleted during the GL.
 We will thus have `p` inside our solution `S`, but p will be nowhere else in the resulting program.
 If the candidate S will be a model of GL(P, S), it won't then be
 minimal, as it will contain {p}, but its presence will not be needed to
 satisfy any rule. So:
 ===> our candidate S should NOT include p.
 - If p is not in S then, during the GL of our program, we are going to
 delete `not p` from the first rule, which becomes `p :- d.`
 Should we include `d` or not? If we do, then we must also satisfy the
 head `p` -> contradiction/circularity, since we started by assuming that
 `p` should not be in `S`. So:
 =====> we should NOT include `d` in our candidate
 - So, for the next rule
 `q v r :- not d.`
 Since we must not have `d` in our solution, when we apply the GL we would be
 left with just `q v r `.
 We cannot chose `q`, since our set S contain the fact `-q`. SO
 ===> we need to satisfy `r`
 Updating our candidate -> `S = {-q, r}`
- Consider the final rule: `d :- not r.`.
 This rule will be eliminated during the GL, since `r` is in our candidate
 solution. There is nothing else to do.

Final candidate: `S = {-q, r}`

You can check that this is indeed an answer set by computing `GL(P, {-q, r})`.

Are there any other answer sets? No. It's the only answer set, because there
were not other choices that we could have made during the construction of the
candidate S.

intuitively this says
```sparql
SELECT ?ancestor WHERE {
 { ?ancestor :parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 ...
 # To the infinity
 }
```
Of course we cannot write an infinite UNION query to cover all sequences of
`:parentOf` predicates of arbitrary length, so `+` is not just an abbreviation.

Besides *SELECT* queries, there are other query types. E.g.,
*CONSTRUCT*

To build/construct a graph containing all the ancestors of `:david`
```
CONSTRUCT {?x :ancestorOf :david } WHERE {?x :parentOf+ :david }
```
The result of a CONSTRUCT query is not a table, but an RDF graph (in Turtle or
other formats).

Reminder. Intuitively:
- `:parentOf+` is the transitive closure of `:parentOf`
- `:parentOf*` is the reflexive-transitive closure of `:parentOf`

# rdf:type vs rdfs:subClassOf

Let's say that
 :Student represents the set Student = {carol, alice}
 :Person represents the set Person = {carol, alice, bob}

:Student rdfs:subClassOf :Person
means that
 Student ⊆ Person
I.e., Student is a subset of Person,
i.e., every element of Student is also an element of Person

:carol rdf:type :Student
means that
 carol ∈ Student
i.e., carol is an element of Student

:Student rdf:type :Person
would mean that
 Student ∈ Person
i.e., the set Student is an element of the set Person
Which is incorrect

# Domain and range

Let's say :purchase represents the binary relation
purchase = { (alice, animals),
 (bob, meddle) }

(which can be represented as
 :alice :purchase :animals .
 :bob :purchase :meddle . )

Then:
domain(purchase) = {alice, bob}
range(purchase) = {animals, meddle}

:purchase rdfs:domain :Person
means that the domain of purchase is Person,
which means that
 domain(purchase) = {alice, bob} ⊆ Person
and so
-> alice ∈ Person (:alice rdf:type :Person)
-> bob ∈ Person (:bob rdf:type :Person)

:purchase rdfs:range :MusicAlbum
means that the range of purchase is the set MusicAlbum
which means that
 range(purchase) = {animals, meddle} ⊆ MusicAlbum
and so
-> animals ∈ MusicAlbum (:animals rdf:type :MusicAlbum)
-> meddle ∈ MusicAlbum (:meddle rdf:type :MusicAlbum)

Exercise 2

 How to express in DL that Alice and Bob are the only children of Carol?
 We already know hasChild(carol, alice) and hasChild(carol, bob).

 The expression
 ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}
 denotes the class of entities all of whose children are inside the set {alice, bob}
 In other words, if x belongs to ∀hasChild.{alice, bob} and y is a child of
 x, then y must belong to the set {alice, bob}, which means that y=alice or y=bob.

 To state that carol belongs to this class we can use a DL concept assertion:
 ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}(carol)
 Or we define some class C = ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}
 and then say C(carol).

 So, together with the facts above (hasChild(carol, alice) and
 hasChild(carol, bob)), the assertion C(carol) lets us express that alice and
 bob are children of carol, and her *only* children.

## OWL/DL Geo Ontology Modeling

### Expressing functionality and inverse functionality in DL

Express that `partOf` is functional using DL syntax.
"`partOf` is functional" means:
- Every entity is linked to at most one thing through `partOf`
- I.e., every entity is `partOf` at most one thing
- I.e., if something is an entity, then it is `partOf` at most one thing
In DL:
```
⊤ ⊑ ≤1 partOf.⊤
```

Express that `capitalOf` is inverse functional using DL syntax:
`⊤ ⊑ ≤1 capitalOf-.⊤`
In this case we use `-` to take the inverse of the `capitalOf` relation, and
then the axiom is the same as functionality.

Another way to see it: `capitalOf` being inverse functional means that any
entity has at most one capital. So we could define `hasCapital` as the inverse
of `capitalOf`:
 `hasCapital = capitalOf-`
And then say that `hasCapital` is functional:
 `⊤ ⊑ ≤1 hasCapital.⊤`
If we substitute `hasCapital` with its definition (`capitalOf-`), we get again
the inverse functionality axiom for `capitalOf`.
 `⊤ ⊑ ≤1 capitalOf-.⊤`

### DL: ranges and local ranges

Express ranges in DL: the range of `genericPartOf` is `GeoEntity`
```
⊤ ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.GeoEntity
```

Local ranges:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Region` for `City`. I.e.:
If something is a `City`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Region`
```
City ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Region
```

Similarly:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Country` for `Region`. I.e.:
If something is a `Region`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Country`
```
Region ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Country
```

Similarly:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Continent` for `Country`. I.e.:
If something is a `Country`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Continent`
```
Country ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Continent
```

What's the meaning of `∀ directorOf.Horror(alfred).` ?

1. Every `Horror` is directed by `alfred`: NO
2. `alfred` has directed only `Horror`s: YES

Semantics of the universal restriction:
`∀ directorOf.Horror = { x ∈ Δ | whenever y ∈ Δ and (x, y) ∈ directorOf, then y ∈ Horror }`

So,`∀ directorOf.Horror(alfred).` means that:
- whenever an entity `y` in our domain is such that
 `alfred` is the `directorOf` `y`
- then `y` must be a `Horror`

I.e., If something is directed by `alfred`, then it is a `Horror`

In other words: "Alfred directs only Horrors"

 that are inside the concept `Horror`. I.e., entities who direct only
 `Horror`s

 that are inside the concept `{memento}`. I.e., entities who have directed only
 `memento`.
- `∀ directorOf.{memento}(chris)`: `chris` has only directed `memento`

How to express that the domain of `directedBy` is `Movie`?

Solution:
```
∃ directedBy.⊤ ⊑ Movie .
```
Intuitively: if an entity is directed by something, then it is a Movie.

Why does this work?
- If `directedBy(psycho, alfred)`
- Then `∃directedBy.⊤(psycho)`
- And then by our solution above `Movie(psycho)`
 [There was a typo here during the lecture: `Movie(movie)`. Sorry!]

What about the other direction?
This axiom:
`Movie ⊑ ∃ directedBy.⊤ .`
has a very different meaning: if an entity is a `Movie`, then it is directed by
some entity. E.g., if
`Movie(vertigo)`
there must be some entity `x` such that `vertigo` is `directedBy` `x`.

### Expressing ranges in DL

How to express that the range of `directedBy` is `Director`?
We need to find a DL expression that means that
- Whenever we have that an entity`x` is `directedBy` an entity `y`,
- Then `y` is a `Director` .

Solution:
```
 ∃ directedBy-.⊤ ⊑ Director .
```
This works because, e.g.:
- if `directedBy(vertigo, alfred)`
- then `directedBy-(alfred, vertigo)`
- and so `∃ directedBy-.⊤(alfred)`
- and by our solution `Director(alfred)`

Short parenthesis on the "intuitive/natural language" reading of existential and
universal quantifiers:
This DL axiom:
 `Movie ⊑ ∃ directedBy.Director ⊓ ∃ starring.Actor`
in natural language means:
 Every movie is directed by *some* Director and it stars *some* Actor
or

Exercise 3 fixing the inconsistent ontology

Why is the ontology inconsistent? Because of this axiom:
```
HappyParent = ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

```
∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
is the set of entities such that all of their children are happy people.

But what if an entity does not have any children? Then trivially all of their
children are happy people, and by the axiom above they must be an `HappyParent`.
Which of course does not make sense.

Different ways to fix the ontology:
```
HappyParent = Parent ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson (where Parent = ∃ hasChild.⊤)
HappyParent = ∃ hasChild.⊤ ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
HappyParent = ∃ hasChild.Person ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

In general, avoid this kind of axiom:
```
C = ∀ R.D
```

Note:
```
HappyParent = ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
is an abbreviation for
```
HappyParent ⊑ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
HappyParent ⊒ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

The first of these inclusions is OK:
```
HappyParent ⊑ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
means that if something is an `HappyParent`, then all of their children are
`HappyPerson`s

The second inclusion is the problem:
```
HappyParent ⊒ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
Means that if all of the children of an entity are `HappyPerson`s, then this
entity is an `HappyParent`. This is the source of the issues above.

So again, the way to fix the axiom is:
```
HappyParent ⊒ Parent ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
Where `Parent = ∃ hasChild.⊤`.

Calculus – Part 2

Prof. Luca Rondi

Programme — academic year 2024/2025

Integration of functions of one variable.
Definite integrals and method of exhaustion. Definition of integrable functions and
classes of integrable functions: integrability of monotone functions and of continuous
functions. Properties of the definite integrals: monotonicity, mean theorem, integra-
bility of the sum, product, absolute value of integrable functions, additivity with
respect to the integration domain. Integrability of functions with a finite number of
discontinuities. Indefinite integrals. Fundamental theorem of integral calculus. Inte-
gration methods: integration by parts and by substitution. Integration of rational
functions.

Topology in Euclidean spaces.
Definition of distance. Definition of neighbourhoods, open sets, closed sets. Definition
of the interior, closure and boundary of a set. Definition of adherent, accumulation
and isolated points. Properties and characterizations of closed and open sets.

Differential calculus in several variables.
Partial derivatives and directional derivatives. Differentiable functions. Jacobian ma-
trix and gradient. Tangent space to the graph. Continuity of partial derivatives im-
plies differentiability. Differential of the composition of maps (chain rule). Mean
value theorem and its consequences. Higher order derivatives and Hessian matrix.
Taylor formula of order 2.

Maximum and minimum problems.
Necessary and sufficient conditions for local maxima and minima. Implicit func-
tion theorem. Geometric properties of the gradient and of level sets. Constrained
minimum problems. Lagrange multiplier theorem.

Multiple integrals. Definition of Riemann integral in several variables. Peano-
Jordan measure: measurable sets and sets of measure 0. Properties of the integral
and of the measure. Reduction theorem and applications: integration on normal
regions in the plane; integration by lines and by planes in the space. Change of
variables: polar coordinates in the plane and spherical and cylindrical coordinates
in the space. Guldino theorem.

Top-down and bottom-up processing
• Inspired by the schema theory, Neisser (1967) identified two main types
 of input processing, known as top-down and bottom-up processing.

• Top-down processing involves the generation of schemas by the higher
 cortical structures, and these schemas are sent down the nervous
 system for comparison with the incoming stimulus. Top-down processing
 is also sometimes referred to as schema-driven or conceptually driven
 processing.

• Top-down (or schema-driven) processing Processing which makes use of
 stored knowledge and schemas to interpret an incoming stimulus
 (contrasts with bottom-up processing).

• Bottom-up (or stimulus-driven) processing Processing which is directed
 by information contained within the stimulus (contrasts with top-down
 processing).

Top-down and bottom-up processing

• Bottom-up processing is initiated by stimulation at
 the ‘bottom end’ of the nervous system (i.e. the
 sense organs), which then progresses up towards
 the higher cortical areas.
• Bottom-up processing is also known as stimulus-
 driven or data-driven processing, because it is the
 incoming stimulus which triggers an appropriate
 form of processing.

 Cognitive Psychology

Information storage in the brain

• Later research supporting Hebb’s proposal
 • Short-term storage involves the strengthening of pre-existing
 synaptic connections, whereas long-term storage involves the
 growth of new synaptic connections between the neurons
 (Bailey & Kandel, 2004).
 • Brain-imaging techniques such as PET scans have also
 confirmed that memory storage and retrieval do in fact
 coincide with the activation of large-scale neural networks,
 spread diffusely through the brain (Habib et al., 2003).
 • Memory storage depends on the growth and plasticity of
 neural connections (De Zeeuw, 2007)
 • The activation-dependent modification of synaptic strength is
 probably the mechanism of memory storage in the brain (Hart
 & Kraut, 2007).

Looked but failed to see accidents

• But what if it is difficult or impossible to discriminate an
 object from its background?
 • The visual system may sense the light reflected from that
 object (so you could argue that the system has ‘detected’ it)
 but the light from the object, and the light from the

• Sensory conspicuity The extent to which aspects of a

What is attention and why do we need it

• So, why does change blindness occur? Why do we not
  process everything?
• The short answer is ‘Because we can’t’.
• Kahneman (1973) proposed the idea of human
  cognition incorporating a central processor allocating
  limited resources to different aspects of the world.
  There are insufficient resources available to process
  everything and so some things will not be processed –
  at least not fully. That is, we do not attend to
  everything.
• Kahneman (2011) makes the point that the phrase
  ‘paying attention’ is very apt. We have limited cognitive
  resources, just as most of us have limited money. We
  cannot ‘pay attention’ to everything.

Multistore models of memory

• STM refers to the memories which are currently
 receiving our conscious attention, and it is a temporary
 store of very brief duration and limited capacity.
• LTM refers to the memories which are not presently in
 conscious awareness, but which are held in storage
 ready to be recalled. The LTM store has a very large
 capacity and can hold information for a lifetime.
• => Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) used these ideas to
 develop a very famous theoretical model of memory

Multistore models of memory

• Atkinson and Shiffrin model dual store of memory,
 • information is held in STM by continually rehearsing it,

The nature and function of memory
• LTM is of extreme importance in everyday life
 • enables us to store information and experiences in a lasting fashion, for
 possible retrieval at some point in the future -> fundamental to all
 aspects of cognition, and crucial to our ability to function properly as
 human beings.
 • We can understand and deal with future situations on the basis of past
 experience.
 • The processes of thinking and problem-solving also rely heavily on the
 use of previous experience,
 • Makes it possible for us to acquire language and to communicate with
 others.
 • Plays a very basic part in the process of perception.
 • Shapes our social interactions with others
• Our very identity relies on an intact memory, and the ability to
 remember who we are and the things that we have done. Almost
 everything we ever do depends on our ability to remember the
 past.

 Cognitive Psychology

The nature and function of memory

• The memory process can be divided into three main
 stages
 • Input stage: newly perceived information is being learned
 or encoded into memory.
 • Storage stage: information is held in preparation for some
 future occasion
 • Output stage: information is retrieved from storage.

 Cognitive Psychology

Figure 6.1 The encoding, storage, and retrieval stages of memory.

The nature and function of memory

• A memory trace will only be retrievable if all three
 of these stages are successfully completed.
• => when we find we are unable to recall some item,
 the cause could be either
 • a failure at the input stage (i.e. learning failure),
 • a failure at the output stage (i.e. retrieval failure),
 • a failure of the storage mechanism.
• In practice, storage failures probably do not occur
 unless there is damage to the brain, so it is probable
 that most forgetting is caused by either learning
 failure or retrieval failure.

Co-ordinating conversations
• The management of turn-taking in conversation is very important
  (smooth even in phone conversations of complete strangers).
• The vast majority of intervals between talker turns in conversation
  fall within a range of +/– 150ms. Speed far faster than if turns

complete sentences

1. A Document Collection: A static set of documents (the corpus) to be searched.

2. A Set of Topics (Queries): A set of formal descriptions of information needs (often including a title,
               description, and narrative) that represent what a user might search for.

3. Relevance Judgments (Ground Truth): A binary or graded list indicating which documents are
               relevant to which topics.
           These components are typically created through a rigorous process, such as those used by TREC (Text
           REtrieval Conference). First, documents are crawled or gathered to form the corpus. Then, domain
           experts or organizers formulate the queries. Crucially, the relevance judgments are created by human
           assessors. Since it is impossible to judge millions of documents for every query, a technique called
           Pooling is often used: the top k results from various different search systems are merged into a "pool,"
           and only these documents are judged by humans. Any document not in the pool is assumed to be
           irrelevant.
           Regarding the second part of the question, Precision@1 (P@1) is the preferred metric for Navigational
           Queries (or Known-Item Search). A classic example is a user searching for "Facebook login" or asking a
           digital assistant (like Siri) "What is the capital of Italy?". In these specific tasks, the user has a single,
           correct destination in mind or requires one specific fact. The user experience is binary: if the first result is
           correct, the system succeeds; if the user has to scroll to the second result, the system has failed to
           provide the instant access expected. Therefore, measuring how often the very first item is relevant is the
           only metric that truly reflects user satisfaction in this context.

 Deterministic segmentation – st

1. Initialization: A random selection of observations from the dataset is made to serve as
   the initial centroids for the current iteration.

2. Assignment: Each observation is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is most similar
(closest in distance) to the observation itself.

3. Convergence Check: If no observations are reassigned to a different cluster compared to
the previous step, the algorithm terminates, having reached convergence.

4. Update and Iteration: Otherwise, a new centroid is calculated for each cluster as the
mathematical average of all observations currently belonging to it. The process then
returns to Step 2.

This algorithm is highly sensitive to outliers, which can significantly skew the average
values and displace centroids from their optimal positions. Conducting a thorough data
cleaning process beforehand is strongly recommended.

 Traditional methodological approach 1

Assuming a common time unit (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly), let m represent average
spending, f average purchase frequency, and t the average customer lifetime. Customer
revenue (r) is then obtained as r = m × f.

 CLTV = r*t = (mf)*t

In order to distinguish revenues from profits, we define p as the company’s profit margin and
explicitly include it in the Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV) formulation:

 CLTV = r*t*p = ((mf)*t*p)

Then we can introduce the discount rate i, an interest applied to reduce future cash flows
(e.g. usually around 10% per year) and a churn rate c, i.e. the percentage of customers who
leaving the company in the period:

 (1−𝑐)
 CLTV = r*p*t *( 1+𝑖 −(1−𝑐) )
